An album written by a player of this instrument contains a solo for it that begins its first track, "Better Git it in Your Soul," and later contains a piece named for a Governor, "Fables for (*) Faubus."A player of this instrument composed albums such as Pithecanthropus Erectus and one titled for his last name "Ah um," named Charles Mingus. For 10 points, What jazz instrument is often played by plucking strings upright?

An album by this man begins with an adapted version of an adagio melody played by the English Horn and was inspired by Alan Lomax recordings. This man's most famous piece switches between intervals on a D and E flat Dorian Scale, and he collaborated with Chick Corea on albums such as Nefertiti. This man took recordings from (*) Joaquin Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez in one album, and included the tracks "Move" and "Boplicity" in another. This creator of Sketches of Spain included the tracks "Blue in Green" and "Freddie Freeloader" in a five track album pioneering modal jazz. For 10 points, name this trumpeter on Kind of Blue.

This album's drummer was Jimmy Cobb, who played in its composer's "first great sextet." The first song recorded for this album features Wynton Kelly on the piano instead of Bill Evans. This album, which contains (*) "Freddie Freeloader," features saxophonists Cannonball Adderley and John Coltrane, and its usage of modal jazz can be heard in its most famous song, "So What." For 10 points, name this best-selling album by Miles Davis.

A version of one of this man's songs that was originally titled "I Need You So" became the theme of the Cootie Williams Orchestra. Miles Davis titled his first Columbia Records album in reference to a song by this musician that Davis performed at the 1955 Newport Jazz Festival. This man plays an E-flat minor 7 chord to begin the first song on an album based on his earliest sessions with Blue Note, which billed him as the (*) "Genius of Modern Music." This man's playing style was noted for heavy use of split notes, sharp hand angles, and strong dissonance. He wrote the most-recorded standard written by a jazz musician, as well as "Epistrophy" and "Straight, No Chaser." For 10 points, name this jazz pianist who wrote "'Round Midnight."

Nick Lucas was the first solo musician to make recordings playing this instrument. The 1972 album Solo Flight contains all of the surviving recordings made by a pioneer of this instrument named Charlie Christian, who may have coined the term "bebop." With Stephane Grappelli, a player of this instrument recorded such hits as "Minor Swing" and "Nuages" (noo-AHZH). In a jazz band, this instrument and the piano are often responsible for (*) comping, or improvising chords to accompany soloists. Prominent players of this instrument include Wes Montgomery and Pat Metheny (muh-THEE-nee). A player of this instrument who pioneered "gypsy jazz" was one of the first to use it to play single-note solos. For 10 points, name this instrument played by Django Reinhardt that has six strings.

This country is home to an albino multi-instrumentalist musician named Hermeto. Horace Silver claimed to have heard his "father's song" while visiting this country, whose music inspired Silver's track "Song for My Father." Instruments such as the cabasa ("cah-BAH-sah") shaker and surdo ("SUR-doo") drum are used in a style of dance in this country which is typically notated in 2/4 ("two-four") time, much like this country's (*) choro ("SHOW-roo") music. Stan Getz popularized a genre of music from this country in his song "The Girl from Ipanema" and worked with its native composers Antonio Carlos Jobim ("zhoh-BEEM") and Joao Gilberto ("zhuh-WOW zheew-BARE-too"). For 10 points, name this Latin American country whose bossa nova music is rooted in the samba dance, and where you can still hear both in Rio de Janeiro.
1.r: Brazil [accept Federative Republic of Brazil or Republica Federativa do Brasil]

1.q: A 2001 Columbia release of the "complete sessions" from one of this man's albums includes the new track "Splashdown" as well as the track "Mademoiselle Mabry" first recorded for Filles de Kilimanjaro. Another album by this man was created for a Bill Clayton documentary about a boxer and consists of the tracks "Right Off" and "Yesternow." That album, Jack Johnson, like this artist's preceding Teo Macero-produced album In a (*) Silent Way, features Chick Corea and John McLaughlin. This man's Second Great Quintet disbanded before his "electric" period, exemplified by an album beginning with a "Pharaoh's Dance" titled Bitches Brew. For 10 points, name this trumpeter whose First Great Quintet recorded Kind of Blue.

The album Reflections was a collection of adaptations of Thelonious Monk's music for this instrument by bebop performer Steve Lacy. The bossa nova hit "The Girl from Ipanema" features Stan Getz on this instrument. Dizzy Gillespie played the piano in a piece written by a player of this instrument that was based on Ray Noble's "Cherokee." That piece, one of the first bebop pieces, was (*) "Ko-ko." Another man who played this instrument improvised over the tune of "My Favorite Things," and included rapid key changes in his "Giant Steps." For 10 points, name this instrument, played by Charlie "Bird" Parker and John Coltrane.

The group that recorded this album frequently used one of its tracks to end concerts like the one recorded in their 1963 album At Carnegie Hall, with members gradually leaving the stage until only the drummer remained. A sequel to this album contains the tracks "Maori Blues" and "Unsquare Dance" and adds the word "further" to the title of this album. During a State-Department-sponsored Eurasian tour, this album's artist was inspired by the (*) rhythms of Turkish street music to write its opening track. A best-selling single on this album was originally intended as a drum solo for Joe Morello and is in 5/4 time. "Blue Rondo alla Turk" and "Take Five" appear on, for 10 points, what Dave Brubeck Quartet album named for its distinctive time signatures?

One player of this instrument formed a namesake sextet featuring Billy Kyle and Charlie Shavers, which specialized in "chamber jazz". Another player of this instrument was part of the original Oscar Peterson Trio alongside Herb Ellis. It was played by the composer of "Stop! Look! And Sing Songs of Revolutions!", which appears on the album The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady. The Blue Devils were formed by a player of this instrument, before he became part of Count Basie's (*) rhythm section alongside Freddie Green and Jo Jones. One player of it wrote a tribute to Lester Young called "Goodbye Porkpie Hat" on an album titled [his name] Ah Um. For 10 points, name this string instrument played by Charlie Mingus, which is normally played upright.

This musician inserted his own name into a hit cover of a song from a Jerry Herman musical, in which he sang that the title character "ain't goin' away again." While a part of one ensemble, this musician performed "Potato Head Blues" and the "Weatherbird Duet" with Earl Hines. This musician's (*) Hot Five preceded another group this musician called his "All-Stars," with which he performed "Hello Dolly," as well as a song in which he sang about "trees so green, red roses too." For 10 points, name this jazz trumpeter and cornetist, nicknamed "Satchmo," who performed "What A Wonderful World."

Duke Ellington and Billy Strayhorn composed a "Portrait of" this artist for Ellington's "Songbook." In a performance in West Berlin, this artist improvised lyrics to the jazz standard "Mack the Knife." This artist recorded "(If You Can't Sing It) You'll Have to Swing It (Mr. Paganini)" with the Chick Webb orchestra. Besides her eight albums covering the (*) Great American Songbook, this artist collaborated with Louis Armstrong on a cover of "Summertime" from Porgy and Bess. This artist included her signature scat singing on songs like "A-Tisket, A-Tasket." For 10 points, name this "First Lady of Song."

A song set in this state spells out the names of many of its ghost towns and notes, "I tremble with the nervous thought / of having been at last forgot." A serial killer from this state is described as having "killed 10,000 people / with the slight of his hand"; that "Clown Killer" is John Wayne Gacy. One song set in this state has a 5/4 beginning referencing the first (*) Ferris Wheel at the World's Columbian Exposition, and a second section about Carl Sandburg. An album named for this state contains "A Short Reprise for Mary Todd." For 10 points, what second state in the Fifty States Project names a Sufjan Stevens album with songs like "Chicago"?

Note to players: Description acceptable. This band's performers first appeared in film playing in the movie Black and Tan, including its 15-year clarinetist Barney Bigard. Ray Nance, a member of this band, usually performed an oft-replicated trumpet solo for one of its signature songs. This band performed the track "Caravan" composed by one of its members, trombonist Juan Tizol, as well as a song titled for the fastest way to get to (*) Sugar Hill in Harlem. This band, which gained fame through performances at New York's "Cotton Club," played songs like "Mood Indigo" and a Billy Strayhorn-composed, transit-inspired standard. For 10 points, name this jazz ensemble that often performed "Take the "A" Train," led by a pianist with a regal name.
1.r: Duke Ellington Orchestra [accept any answer referring to Duke Ellington’s jazz band or Duke Ellington's jazz ensemble or Duke Ellington’s orchestra; accept Edward Kennedy Ellington in place of Duke Ellington]

1.q: Due to his strange sounds on albums such as The Golden 8, one player of this instrument at Minton's playhouse was given the nickname "Klook." With Clifford Brown, one player of this instrument created tracks such as "Powell's Prances" on an album set "At Basin Street." A hard bop player of this instrument recorded albums such as A Night at Birdland and Moanin' with his "Jazz Messengers." A (*) "battle" between two famous players of this instrument at Carnegie Hall was set to the music of "Sing, Sing, Sing," which also includes a lengthy solo for it. Max Roach and Art Blakey were two players of this instrument, which plays an extremely long solo in the middle of Dave Brubeck's "Take Five." Single-stroke rolls and the hi-hat are commonly utilized in soloes of this instrument. For 10 points, name this most common jazz percussion instrument.

In 1938, this person was chosen as the lead singer for Artie Shaw's band, but quit after being asked to use the service elevator at the Lincoln Hotel in New York City. This singer frequently collaborated with Lester Young and sang the first commercially successful version of the song (*) "Summertime" from George Gershwin's Porgy and Bess. One of her best-known recordings refers to the title objects "swinging in the Southern breeze" and "hanging from the poplar trees." For 10 points, name this African-American woman, who described the aftermath of a lynching in "Strange Fruit."

This genre of music experienced a revival in the 1990s with the rise of Royal Crown Revue. Louis Armstrong once said "If you don't feel [this genre], you'll never know it," and it was popular at the Savoy Ballroom, where the (*) Lindy Hop was often danced to it. This type of music was performed by Fletcher Henderson and Glenn Miller, and Louis Prima wrote a song in this style made popular by a 1937 performance at Carnegie Hall. That song was "Sing Sing Sing." For 10 points, name this style of jazz that Benny Goodman was the "king of."

The first section of an album by this artist opens with an "F A-flat, F B-flat" motif by Jimmy Garrison on the double bass, before this artist chants the album's title nineteen times following that same motif. The title track of one of this composer's songs features extended solos over E major and minor chords with McCoy Tyner. That track by this artist was inspired by a song from a Rodgers and Hammerstein musical. This musician included the song "Lazy Bird" on his album (*) Blue Train. Chord progressions that follow chromatic third relations are called this composer's "changes." Critic Ira Gitler referred to this musician's style as "sheets of sound." The sound of a gong opens this saxophonist's A Love Supreme. For 10 points, name this jazz saxophonist of Giant Steps.

For the original version of a song by a player of this instrument, the band sings "Oh, Lord, don't let 'em shoot us!" and yells throughout the piece. A version of that composition appears on an album by the same player of this instrument, which opens with the track "Better Git It In Your Soul." A track on Giant Steps named after a player of this instrument opens with a C minor 7th chord; that track is (*) "Mr. PC." The opening notes of Miles Davis's "So What" were played by Paul Chambers on this instrument. A famous bandleader who played this instrument created an album named after himself, followed by the syllables "Ah Um." For 10 points, name this instrument played by Charles Mingus, which is low-pitched, stringed, and played upright.

J. R. Monterose and Jackie McLean use their saxophones to imitate foghorns and cars on this musician's cover of Gershwin's "A Foggy Day." That song appears on a 1956 album by this musician whose cover depicts a white, orange, and black humanoid figure. Long, one-chord vamps performed by this musician's Jazz Workshop were developed into tracks like (*) "Haitian Fight Song." An album by this artist is titled after the original scientific name of Java Man. This musician, who titled one album after his last name five times, included "Fables of Faubus" on a 1959 album that also contains an elegy to Lester Young titled "Goodbye Pork Pie Hat." For 10 points, name this eccentric jazz bassist that recorded an album titled "[him] Ah Um."

A player of this instrument composed "Davenport Blues," and played an influential solo on the Trumbauer Orchestra's version of "Singin' the Blues." The leaders of ODJB and the Creole Jazz Band played this instrument, the smallest to use a device named for Paddy Harmon. This instrument plays an 11-second cadenza at the start of "West End Blues." A player of this instrument led ensembles that recorded (*) "Potato Head Blues" and "Heebie Jeebies." King Oliver mentored a player of this instrument who recorded with the Hot Five and Seven and was nicknamed "Satchmo." For 10 points, name this instrument played by Louis Armstrong.

This musician's early recordings like "I'll Chase the Blues Away" were inspired by Connee Boswell. This musician's nonsense lyrics on "How High the Moon" were included on an album recorded "at Duke's Place." Decca pressured this musician into recording well-known songs like "Lady Be Good" before this musician joined Norman Granz's Verve label. Bobby Darin is namechecked on a cover of "Mack the Knife" by this musician that was recorded live in Berlin. After recording a series of (*) "songbook" albums, this musician recorded duets with Louis Armstrong like 1958's Porgy & Bess. Early in her career, this musician sang "A-Tisket, A-Tasket" for Chick Webb. For 10 points, name this "First Lady of Song" who popularized scat singing.

Joe Brazil's recording of this album performed live in Seattle was released by Impulse Records in 2021. Art Davis and Archie Shepp appear on an alternate take of this album's opening track that omits a vocal chant. On this album's opening track, Jimmy Garrison introduces a four-note bass motif that is later picked up by saxophone. This album followed the release of Crescent, which was also accompanied by the (*) "classic quartet." The second of this album's four tracks, "Resolution," opens with a drum solo by Elvin Jones, while a tam-tam crash opens its first part "Acknowledgement." This album is often interpreted as its artist's declaration of devotion to God. For 10 points, name this 1965 album by John Coltrane.

A bandleader who played this instrument recorded "All the Things You Are" with singer Helen Forrest. That player of this instrument led the Gramercy Five, an example of the "band within a band" concept pioneered by another player of this instrument. A player of this instrument popularized Cole Porter's (*) "Begin the Beguine." Another player of this instrument recorded a piece on which Gene Krupa played an extended drum solo; that piece is originally by Louis Prima and was featured at a 1938 Carnegie Hall performance. For 10 points, Artie Shaw and Benny Goodman played what single-reed woodwind instrument?

This musician's son is the current tenor saxophonist of the Blue Note 7, and their wife played both piano and harp in her album Journey in Satchidananda. This musician's later interest in free jazz led to such Impulse! Records albums as Ascension. This musician's quartet featuring McCoy Tyner and Elvin Jones released an album opening with a gong strike in its movement (*) "Acknowledgement." Descending major thirds form this musician's namesake "changes," employed in the title track of an album featuring "Mr. P.C." and "Naima."Ira Gitler dubbed this musician's improvisations "sheets of sound." For 10 points, name this saxophonist of Giant Steps and A Love Supreme.

A Clint Eastwood biographical film about this musician ends with his death while watching TV with Baroness Nica. It's not Joe Henderson, but this man released a piece referencing his stay in a California state hospital called "Relaxin at Camarillo." One piece by this musician that uses a sequence of ii-V ("two-five") progressions is known as "Blues for Alice." This musician used the chords of (*) Ray Noble's "Cherokee" as inspiration for his "Ko Ko," which, along with "Ornithology," exemplify the fast style of jazz he co-founded with Dizzy Gillespie. For 10 points, name this bebop saxophonist nicknamed "Bird."
1.r: Charlie Parker [accept Bird or Yardbird before “Bird”; prompt on Yardbird after “Bird”]

1.q: Miles Davis' album Bags' Groove features three early compositions by a player of this non-vibraphone instrument, including "Doxy" and "Oleo." An album titled "[this instrument] Madness" features two players of it, one of whom practiced on the Williamsburg Bridge for 15 hours a day. A Bahamian ("buh-HAY-me-in") folk song inspired a player of this instrument to write "St. Thomas," which begins his album "[this instrument] (*) Colossus." A chord progression developed by a player of this instrument cycles through keys a major third apart. Sonny Rollins played this instrument, as did a musician who used the "sheets of sound" style of improvisation on albums like Giant Steps. For 10 points, name this instrument played by John Coltrane.

Ken Burns's Jazz promoted this musician's dubious claim to have met Bix Beiderbecke on a steamboat. Okeh Records published a recording on which this musician legendarily dropped his lyric sheet. Gunther Schuller called this musician "The First Great Soloist" for shifting the focus of jazz from collective to individual improvisation, as shown by his cadenza at the start of his mentor (*) King Oliver's song "West End Blues." This artist wishes "It's so nice to have you back" in the title song of his album Hello, Dolly! This musician's "Hot Seven" recorded "Potato Head Blues," and his "Hot Five" recorded "Heebie Jeebies." For 10 points, scat singing was pioneered by what New Orleans-born trumpeter nicknamed Satchmo?

The album Cookin' with the Miles Davis Quintet introduced the song "Blues by [this word]." Power chords are alternately named for this word due to their intervallic content. This word ends the title of a song whose accompaniment alternates between E-flat minor seven and B-flat minor seven in the rhythm "long-short, long-short, long long." A common jazz progression proceeds from two to this number. Paul (*) Desmond improvised the blues-scale melody of a song titled for this number to show off Joe Morello's ability to play in odd time signatures. A single from Dave Brubeck's album Time Out is titled "Take [this number]." For 10 points, what is one more than the number of beats in the most common time signature?
1.r: five [accept "Blues by Five"; accept five chords or fifth chords; accept "Take Five"]

1.q: These things inspired a "hillbilly" jump blues song written by Milt Gabler and recorded by Louis Jordan in 1946. A riff from "Happy-Go-Lucky Local" inspired a song about these things by Jimmy Forrest. One band's live performances of a song named for these things featured scat-singing by Ray Nance, who played an oft-imitated trumpet solo on its original recording. The film Sun Valley Serenade popularised a (*) Glenn Miller recording of a song named for these things in which the singer talks to a shoeshine boy. A song that describes using one of these things "to go to Sugar Hill way up in Harlem" was written by Billy Strayhorn for Duke Ellington. For 10 points, what vehicles are exemplified by the "Chattanooga Choo-Choo?"
1.r: trains [accept "Night Train" or "Take the A Train"] (The first line is about "Choo Choo Ch'Boogie.")

1.q: A trio led by this musician was joined by Fletcher Henderson's band in a series of "Rhythm Club" concerts given at Congress Hotel. A sonata with a "Romanza" second movement was commissioned by this musician from Francis Poulenc ("poo-LANK"). To impress this musician, guitarist Charlie Christian riffed on the song "Rose Room" for 45 minutes. This man regularly performed on NBC's Let's Dance withpianist (*) Teddy Wilson and bassist Lionel Hampton.This man's racially integrated band rose to fame after it performed "Sing, Sing, Sing" at Carnegie Hall. For 10 points, name this jazz clarinetist lauded as the "King of Swing."

This man told people "get your money back" after they mistakenly paid to see a recording session of his 2 hour-long piece Epitaph. A track by this man was rerecorded as an instrumental version after Columbia Records removed lyrics like "Oh, Lord, don't let 'em shoot us!" This man recorded a tone poem depicting the rise and fall of man, (*) Pithecanthropus Erectus. "Better Git It in Your Soul" opens an album by this man most famous for its track "Fables of Faubus." This man's elegy for Lester Young, "Goodbye Pork Pie Hat" appears on an album titled for his name appended by "Ah Um." For 10 points, name this jazz double bassist.

A player of this instrument wrote the track "Calling the Indians Out" to open his oratorio Blood on the Fields, which was the first jazz composition to win the Pulitzer Prize in music. Another player of this instrument recorded songs for King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band, including a track which opens with a cadenza with this instrument, "West End Blues." One player of this instrument was the lead performer on the tracks (*) "Freddie Freeloader" and "So What." That artist recorded his album Kind of Blue with his namesake First Great Quintet. For 10 points, name this brass instrument played by Miles Davis and Louis Armstrong.
1.r: trumpet (the musician mentioned in the first two lines is Wynton Marsalis)

1.q: A musician from this country commemorated a fellow trumpet player's death with his album I Remember Clifford. A percussionist from this country recorded Herbie Hancock's "Watermelon Man" in its signature boogaloo style. One musician collaborated with Gil Fuller and a percussionist from this country on a jazz standard inspired by this country's (*) mambo melodies. That standard is Dizzy Gillespie's "Manteca." This country's genre of pregons or "street vendor cries" is exemplified by the Moises Simons song "The Peanut Vendor." For 10 points, claves and bongos are used in the traditional music of what Caribbean country?

In this piece, which is in march form, the syncopated line "E-flat, D, D-flat, C, B-flat" is played in high octaves in the section before a D-flat major trio. This was the first and most successful piece by its composer printed by John Stark. This A-flat major piece opens a Nonesuch Records album by (*) Joshua Rifkin that revived interest in its genre. This piano piece sold over a million copies in its composer's lifetime and made him the "King of Ragtime." For 10 points, name this Scott Joplin rag likely named for a Sedalia nightclub.

Ben Webster and a player of this instrument co-name a compilation album of Duke Ellington's band; that player is Jimmy Blanton. Another player of this instrument used "Haitian Fight Song" to open his album The Clown and recorded a tone poem depicting the rise of man, (*) Pithecanthropus Erectus. In Miles Davis's first quintet, this instrument was played by Paul Chambers. "Goodbye Pork Pie Hat" is on an album named for a player of this instrument and the Latin pun "Ah Um." For 10 points, Charles Mingus played what lowest common stringed instrument?

A live performance of this album in Seattle, featuring Pharoah Sanders, was released in 2021 by Impulse! Records. The opening track from this album is built around an (read slowly) F, A-flat, F, B-flat motif, which is played first by double bass, then tenor saxophone, before finally becoming a vocal chant. This album, recorded by its artist's so-called "classic quartet," ends with a track meant to accompany a (*) devotional poem in the liner notes titled "Psalm." A tam-tam strike opens this album's first track, "Acknowledgement." This album was recorded five years after Giant Steps. For 10 points, name this best-selling album by John Coltrane.

A player of this instrument collaborated with Bill Evans on the 1962 album Undercurrent. The 1972 album Solo Flight contains nearly all the extant live recordings by a man who played this instrument in Benny Goodman's Sextet. The fourth track on Miles Davis' Bitches Brew is named for a player of this instrument who founded the group Mahavishnu Orchestra. This instrument, popularized by (*) Charlie Christian, was played by the composer of "Nuages" and "Minor Swing," who together with violinist Stephane Grappelli founded Paris's Quintette du Hot Club. For 10 points, Django Reinhardt played what stringed instrument?
1.r: jazz guitar (the artist in the first line is Jim Hall; the Miles Davis track is named after John McLaughlin.)

1.q: Music from this country inspired the rhythm of the accompaniment to a song whose singer asks "Don't you notice how / I get quiet when there's no one else around?" A 1962 Vince Guaraldi album is titled for "Jazz Impressions" of a film scored by composers from this country. A standard that celebrates "quiet nights of quiet stars" appears after "Desafinado" on an album partially titled for a (*) guitarist from this country. A standard from this country about a "tall and tan and young and lovely" woman opens Getz/Gilberto("Getz jeew-BARE-too"). For 10 points, name this country whose bossa nova style is exemplified by "The Girl from Ipanema."
1.r: Brazil [or Federative Republic of Brazil; or República Federativa do Brasil] (The first line refers to Laufey’s song “From the Start.”)

1.q: This song is based on the repeated chord progression [read slowly]C minor, A-flat 7, G7 flat 9. Barney Josephson required that performances of this song use only a single spotlight on its singer's face at the Cafe Society. The first recording of this song begins with seventy seconds of piano improvisation by Sonny White. A poem by Abel Meeropol was used for this song's lyrics, which invokes the (*) "gallant South." This song describes a tree with "blood on the leaves" and "blood at the root." For 10 points, name this anti-lynching song popularized by Billie Holiday.

This musician composed the reverie Villa d'Este for his classical album Fantasies & Delusions. A song by this musician begins with an ascending, then descending "C, C-sharp, D" motif, followed by the notes "F, down to C." Low broken octave Gs precede "The Ballad of Brenda and Eddie" in a song by this musician that partially inspired Twyla Tharp's musical (*) Movin' Out. C major harmonica solos are interspersed in a song by this musician that begins "It's nine o'clock on a Saturday." "Vienna" is by, for 10 points, what American singer of "Piano Man"?

The "A" section of a song by this musician alternates four bars each of D7 sus ("suhs") and F7 sus, implying the D Phrygian mode. This musician began emphasizing upper structures instead of guide tones after he misheard his bandleader as saying "don't play the butter notes." A silhouetted man sails a boat on the cover of an album by this musician, who still performs publicly at age 86. This musician composed "Dolphin Dance" and "Maiden Voyage" while playing (*) piano in Miles Davis' "Second Great Quintet." This pianist reinterpreted a bluesy song from his album Takin' Off on a 1973 album recorded with his jazz-rock fusion band, the Headhunters. For 10 points, name this composer of "Chameleon" and "Watermelon Man."
1.r: Herbie Hancock [or Herbert Jeffrey Hancock] (The first clue refers to “Maiden Voyage.” Miles Davis actually told him “don’t play the bottom notes,” i.e. the root of the chord.)

1.q: In an early use of tritone substitution, the intro to a song by this musician alternates between E-flat 7 and D minor 6 chords over a syncopated bass line. This musician recorded that song with Sarah Vaughan under its original title, "Interlude." This bandleader, who mentored Arturo Sandoval, co-wrote an early standard based on a two-three son clave("SOHN KLAH-vay") with Chano Pozo. This American pioneered (*) Afro-Cuban jazz through the mambo-influenced composition "Manteca" and the angular melody of "A Night in Tunisia." This musician and his close friend Charlie Parker are traditionally credited with developing bebop. For 10 points, name this musician who played a bent trumpet with puffed-out cheeks, nicknamed "Dizzy."

Musicians like Black Coffee blend house music with an electronic genre from this country based around synthesized log drums. The Mahotella Queens are a vocal group from this country who collaborated with a low-voiced singer known as a "groaner." A singer from this country popularized a song that claims "everybody starts to move as soon as Pata Pata starts to play." (*) Paul Simon recorded Graceland with Ladysmith Black Mambazo, a group from this country. The Tokens adapted a folk song from this country into "The Lion Sleeps Tonight." This country's genre of mbaqanga ("MM-bah-KAHNG-guh") was performed by Hugh Masekela and Miriam Makeba. For 10 points, amapiano("AH-muh-pee-AH-noh") is from what country whose music is influenced by Zulu and Xhosa traditions?
1.r: South Africa [or Republic of South Africa or RSA; or Ningizimu Afrika, Mzantsi Afrika, Suid- Afrika, Afrika Borwa, Afrika Dzonga, Afurika Tshipembe, or Sewula Afrika]

1.q: Bill Evans repeatedly played a song that is originally from this work while grieving Scott LaFaro's death. Gil Evans wrote "Gone" for an album by Miles Davis based on this work, whose first track is "Buzzard Song." In their last album, Louis Armstrong and Ella Fitzgerald covered songs from this work such as one that lists "things that you're liable / To read in the Bible." Billie Holiday made the first hit recording of a song from this work that features the lyric "One (*) of these mornings / You're going to rise up singing." This work introduced a lullaby about a time when "fish are jumpin' and the cotton is high." For 10 points, "It Ain't Necessarily So" and "Summertime" are from what George Gershwin opera?
1.r: Porgy and Bess (The first line refers to “I Loves You, Porgy.”)

2.q: This musician co-wrote an intro that he plays in an influential recording of the tune "All the Things You Are" that consists of the repeated eighth notes [read slowly] A-A-flat-D-flat and A-flat-G-C. The Coltrane standard "26-2" is a modal version of a tune by this musician. Oboe solos on the B-sections to the tunes "Just Friends" and "I Didn't Know What Time It Was" are included on an album titled "[this musician] with Strings." The drummer (*) Jo Jones allegedly threw a symbol at this musician after he poorly improvised a solo, and he used the chords from "Cherokee" to write the standard "Ko-Ko." For 10 points, name this jazz bebop saxophonist who wrote the standard "Yardbird Suite" and was nicknamed "Bird."
2.r: Charlie Parker (The standards in the first line are “Yardbird Suite” and “Billie’s Bounce”.)

2.q: A player of this instrument recorded the 2023 album Prime with his "New Jawn." That player of this instrument recorded bebop tunes with Stephen Scott and Roy Hargrove on the 1995 album Parker's Mood. A player of this instrument sings the refrain "You get to just keep on getting there" on the track "Earth to Heaven" from the album Emily's D+Evolution [D plus evolution]. A player of this instrument recorded "I X Love" and "II B. S." [Two B.S] on an album whose title is his last name repeated five times. Christian McBride and (*) Esperanza Spalding play this instrument. A player of this instrument recorded "Fables of Faubus" and "Goodbye Pork Pie Hat" on a 1959 album titled [his last name] Ah Um. This instrument can be played with a "walking" style or the "slap" technique. For 10 points, Charles Mingus played what low string instrument?
2.r: bass [accept upright bass; accept double bass; accept bass guitar; accept electric bass]

2.q: This musician claims to have been to "Paris, Beirut, you know, Iraq, Iran, Eurasia" in one song's spoken intro. The chorus of a song by this musician uses the chord progression [read slowly] B major, F minor 11, E major 7, C sharp minor 7, to F sharp sus. A song by this musician depicts a boy "born in hard-time Mississippi" who moves to New York and is imprisoned for a crime he didn't commit. This musician played drums and the room-sized TONTO synth for his albums (*) Innervisions and Talking Book. This musician played an extended harmonica solo in a song dedicated to his daughter Aisha, "Isn't She Lovely," which appears on Songs in the Key of Life. A song by this musician includes the lyric "When you believe in things / That you don't understand / Then you suffer." For 10 points, name this Motown artist of "Sir Duke" and "Superstition."
2.r: Stevie Wonder [or Stevland Hardaway Morris; or Stevland Hardaway Judkins]

2.q: A piece by this composer inspired the tune of the songs Passport and Moose the Mooche by Charlie Parker. A song composed by this person that repeats the phrase "hi-ho, alas" titles an Ahmad Jamal live album recorded at the Pershing Hotel. A piece by this composer inspired a Theolonius Monk song recorded with Art Blakey partially titled "A-Ning," which uses its[One six two five] sequence. After the title Rodgers and (*) Hammerstein track, two songs by this person feature on Coltrane's 1961 album My Favorite Things. This composer of "But Not For Me" described a time when "the living's easy" in another standard. Jazz musicians often improvise from a 32-bar progression by this composer called the rhythm changes. For 10 points, name this composer of "Summertime" from Porgy and Bess and An American in Paris.

A jazz standard written by a player of this instrument that appears on album This Time was set to lyrics by Al Jarreau. That standard by a player of this instrument was introduced on the album Light as a Feather. One player of this instrument was told by Miles Davis not to play "the butter notes" during his solos. That member of Davis' Second Great Quintet who played this instrument wrote the track (*) "Dolphin Dance" for his album Maiden Voyage. Another player of this instrument wrote a standard inspired by the Concierto de Aranjuez. One player of this instrument wrote the standard "Spain" while another wrote "Chameleon" and "Watermelon Man." For 10 points, Chick Corea and Herbie Hancock play which keyboard instrument?

A Clint Eastwood biographical film about this musician ends with his death while watching TV with Baroness Nica. It's not Joe Henderson, but this man released a piece referencing his stay in a California state hospital called "Relaxin at Camarillo." One piece by this musician that uses a sequence of ii-V ("two-five") progressions is known as "Blues for Alice." This musician used the chords of (*) Ray Noble's "Cherokee" as inspiration for his "Ko Ko," which, along with "Ornithology," exemplify the fast style of jazz he co-founded with Dizzy Gillespie. For 10 points, name this bebop saxophonist nicknamed "Bird."
2.r: Charlie Parker [accept Bird or Yardbird before “Bird”; prompt on Yardbird after “Bird”]

2.q: A bandleader who played this instrument recorded "All the Things You Are" with singer Helen Forrest. That player of this instrument led the Gramercy Five, an example of the "band within a band" concept pioneered by another player of this instrument. A player of this instrument popularized Cole Porter's (*) "Begin the Beguine." Another player of this instrument recorded a piece on which Gene Krupa played an extended drum solo; that piece is originally by Louis Prima and was featured at a 1938 Carnegie Hall performance. For 10 points, Artie Shaw and Benny Goodman played what single-reed woodwind instrument?

This musician appears as "Pie-Eye" in Anatomy of a Murder, a film he scored with an orchestra including Jimmy Hamilton. This musician co-wrote a song with trombonist Juan Tizol and recorded it with him in the band Barney Bigard and His Jazzopators. A live concert album by this musician and his band includes a 27-chorus solo played by saxophonist Paul Gonsalves. Members of this musician's band recorded the first version of (*) "Caravan." This musician's career was revitalized by a 1956 live album recorded at the Newport Jazz Festival, where he performed a song written by his collaborator Billy Strayhorn. This musician wrote the songs "In a Sentimental Mood" and "Mood Indigo." For 10 points, name this jazz pianist whose orchestra performed "Take the 'A' Train."

This instrument was played on the original lineup for the Maha•vishnu Orchestra by Rick Laird. This instrument doubles the opening keyboard melody of the Chick Corea song "Got a Match?" as played by John Patitucci. Another player of this instrument asks "you know the lonesome road, don't you?" to the title "Judas" in a track that appears on her album Emily's D+Evolution. After a synth intro, this instrument plays a high melody with drums to open (*) "Birdland." This instrument is played by Esperanza Spalding. Another player of this instrument replaced Miroslav Vitous in the band Weather Report and played one of these instruments "of Doom" with the frets removed. For 10 points, name this instrument played by Jaco Pastorius, a low-pitched guitar.
2.r: bass [or bass guitar; accept double bass or upright bass or string bass; accept Bass of Doom] (All of the clues refer to bass guitar, but the musicians also play double bass.)

2.q: A contrafact of Charlie Parker's "Confirmation" by this musician titled "26-2" was included as a bonus track on the reissue of an album titled [this musician's] Sound. The last surviving copy of a long-lost album by this musician was given to his wife, which was rereleased in 2018 as Both Directions at Once. An album by this musician includes a poem in the liner notes whose words correspond to each note in the melody of its last track, which appears after (*) "Pursuance." A 1960 album by this composer features a contrafact of Miles Davis's "Tune Up" titled "Countdown" and a song titled for this musician's wife's middle name, "Naima." This musician innovated a cycle of modulations separated by major thirds referred to as this musician's namesake "changes." For 10 points, name this jazz saxophonist of Giant Steps.
2.r: John Coltrane [or John William Coltrane; accept Coltrane changes or Coltrane’s Sound]

2.q: Jannis Sturtz founded a record label for music primarily sung in this language, which released the records Jazz, Jazz, Jazz and The SLAM! Years. An uncle who played this language's traditional music inspired the rapid picking of surf musician Dick Dale. This language's music is played by takht ensembles. Exaggerations are generally frowned upon when texts in this language are sung in a (*) taghanni. In the 19th century, this language's music began using an equal temperament system with 24 individually named tones separated by quarter tones, a system called gadwal. This language's word for ascent names the mode system of maqam ("ma-kam"). A word in this language names the medieval instrument called the oud. For 10 points, name this language that is used when melodiously reciting the surahs.

A player of this instrument included his pieces "Dr. Free-Zee" and "Mr. X" on an album first recorded after the death of two of his collaborators. A player of this instrument founded a bebop ensemble to feature the music of Tadd Dameron. That musician recorded the album Together! with another player of this instrument, who lends his name to a "Jazz Machine" and whose debut record features his older brothers Hank and Thad. A player of this instrument and (*) Horace Silver led a group often credited for originating the hard bop genre, whose most famous hit was "Moanin'". The Jazz Messengers were led by Art Blakey, a player of this instrument. For 10 points, Philly Joe Jones, Elvin Jones, and Max Roach played what rhythm section instrument which includes a hi-hat and snare?

European groups that adopted rap elements to this genre in the late '80s include Bomb the Bass and The Beatmasters. That "hip" style of this genre was adopted by acts like C+C Music Factory and the duo behind "It Takes Two." A style of this genre popular during the "Second Summer of Love" is characterized by the squelching sound of the Roland 303. Frankie Knuckles is commonly called "the Godfather of" this genre. A group best known for this (*) disco-derived genre recorded a song that features Giorgio Moroder discussing his career over changing instrumentals. That group moved away from a style of this genre heard on Human After All and Discovery for styles with more live instruments on an album with the songs "Lose Yourself to Dance" and "Instant Crush." For 10 points, name this electronic genre of the album Homework by Daft Punk.
2.r: house [accept hip house, acid house, or French house; prompt on electronic or EDM]

2.q: A genre from this country was greatly popularized by producer Martin Meissonnier on albums such as Synchro System. An artist from this country sued Serge Gainsbourg for failing to credit him for three songs off Drums of Passion, including the widely covered "Jin-go-lo-ba." A musician from this country gives his name to John Coltrane's final live album, which includes a 35-minute version of "My Favorite Things." This country's government raided the artist's commune (*) Kalakuta Republic after the release of protest albums like Expensive Shit and Zombie. King Sunny Ade popularized juju music from this country, the birthplace of drummer Babatunde Olatunji. For 10 points, name this country of Fela Kuti, the father of Afrobeat.

Musicians in one style of music will percussively strike these instruments in the practice of golpe. A style of playing this instrument influenced by the mbira was developed by Chimuranga musician Jonah Sithole, who performed with Jonathan Mapfumo. A musician developed a style of this instrument inspired by the njarka on albums like Savane and Talking Timbuktu. This instrument was the main one played by Malian musician Ali Farka Toure, as well as the founder of TPOK Jazz, (*) Franco Luambo. The baroque precursor to this modern instrument was called the vihuela. Cale Gitano musicians like the band behind the songs "Volare" and "Bamboleo" often play this instrument fingerstyle. For 10 points, name this instrument central to Spanish flamenco music.

Ted Gioia ("GOY-a") recounted a story in which this musician was invited to make a recording with Charlie Parker but refused to play. This musician used a harmon mute on an album that includes a track whose title chord consists of stacked fourths. Electric pianos and guitars feature on tracks like 'Pharaoh's Dance' on this musician's landmark (*) fusion album Bitches Brew. This musician worked with Gil Evans for an album inspired by folk songs from Galicia and Andalusia, which includes an arrangement of the Adagio of Concerto de Aranjuez. For 10 points, name this trumpeter of Sketches of Spain who pioneered cool jazz on Kind of Blue.

The first vocal recording of this song was by Dakota Staton, but an instrumental version featuring Wyatt Ruther and Fats Heard was released three years earlier. A D/Eb ("D over E flat") chord played on the piano accompanies the opening melody of a version of this song recorded by Oscar Peterson. The singer walks slowly towards the microphone to mimic a fade-in effect during the line (*) "on my own" in a 1959 recording of this song by Johnny Mathis. TikTok repopularised a doo-wop cover of this song by Lesley Gore that opens with the acapella line "look at me". Clint Eastwood used an instrumental version of this song in his directorial debut, which was titled Play [this song] For Me. For 10 points, name this jazz standard by Errol Garner, which begins with the singer calling themselves "helpless as a kitten up a tree."

This musician first recorded his contrafact of "Just You, Just Me," titled "Evidence," during his sessions with vibraphonist Milt Jackson, Wizard of the Vibes. This musician was depicted as a French Resistance fighter on an album cover that alludes to his friendship with Rothschild heiress Pannonica de Koenigswarter. 25 separate takes of the notoriously difficult title track were spliced together on an album by this musician that concludes with (*) "Bemsha Swing." This artist's characteristic dissonant chords and chromatic scales can be heard on the pieces "Epistrophy" and "Straight, No Chaser" from his compilation album Genius of Modern Music. For 10 points, name this prolific pianist who released Brilliant Corners and wrote the most-recorded jazz standard of all time, "Round Midnight."
2.r: Thelonious Monk (The album in the second sentence is Underground.)

2.q: The album Black Classical Music was recorded by a player of this instrument, Yussef Dayes. A player of this instrument recorded Landmarks with his namesake Fellowship Band. Brian Blade plays this instrument, as did Jack DeJohnette ("dee-juh-NETT"). A player of this instrument joined the Second Great Quintet at age 17 and later formed his namesake "Lifetime." The Greensboro sit-ins inspired a player of this instrument to record his avant-garde Freedom Now Suite titled (*) We Insist! A player of this non-trumpet instrument recorded "Daahoud" and "Joy Spring" with a quintet that he co-led with Clifford Brown. Tony Williams and Max Roach played this instrument. Buddy Rich advocated for the use of the traditional grip while playing this instrument. For 10 points, name this instrument that includes the hi-hat and snare.

This place titles Nala Sinephro's debut ambient jazz album. Brian Eno drew upon country music and used a steel guitar on "Deep Blue Day," which he recorded for an album inspired by an object from this place. A stylophone drones on C and B as the guitar plays C major and E minor chords in the verse of a song about a person from this place. The octave leap in the chorus of "Somewhere Over the Rainbow" is quoted in a song about a person from this place who is "waiting in the (*) sky." An Afrofuturist jazz musician who donned costumes inspired by Ancient Egypt led his Arkestra in the film [This location] is the Place. An androgynous alter ego from this location first appeared on a glam rock album titled for his band the Spiders and their "Rise and Fall." For 10 points, the singer repeats "Ground Control to Major Tom" in a song titled for what location by David Bowie?
2.r: space [accept outer space or the cosmos or the stars; accept the moon or specific planets such as Mars; accept Space is the Place; accept “Space Oddity” or “Starman”; accept Space 1.8 or Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars; accept Sun Ra; accept Ziggy Stardust]

2.q: Sonny Boy Williamson and a player of this instrument made Helena, Arkansas a musical hotbed with their radio show King Biscuit Time. An iconic lick for this instrument comes from the piece "Dust My Broom," which was recorded without the knowledge of performer Elmore James. Ry Cooder's score for Paris, Texas uses a song on this instrument that appears on the Voyager Golden Record, "Dark Was The Night, Cold Was The Ground" by (*) Blind Willie Johnson. O Brother, Where Art Thou? fictionalizes a player of this instrument who, like another player of this instrument with the same surname, legendarily went to a crossroads to sell his soul to the Devil. For 10 points, name this instrument played by Delta blues musicians Tommy and Robert Johnson.
2.r: acoustic guitar [accept slide guitar; accept bottleneck guitar; accept resonator guitar] (The first sentence refers to Robert Lockwood, Jr., a protege of Robert Johnson; King Biscuit Time is the longest-running daily radio broadcast in American history.)

3.q: Miles Davis plays the piano to accompany this artist on the track "I Know," which was recorded for a collaborative album between this artist and the Modern Jazz Quartet. This artist played with the Max Roach Quartet on an album titled "[this artist] Plus 4". A 12-bar blues standard written by and named for this artist opens with a descending B-flat minor pentatonic scale and consists of a 4-bar riff on that scale repeated three times. The B-side of the Miles Davis album Bags' Groove was the debut of several jazz standards written by this artist, such as (*) "Airegin." For his most famous album, this artist recorded an instrumental version of "Mack the Knife" titled "Moritat." That album also features a song inspired by the calypso music this artist was exposed to during his childhood in the Virgin Islands. "Doxy" and "Oleo" are jazz standards written by -- for 10 points -- what jazz saxophonist who recorded the hit "St. Thomas" for his album Saxophone Colossus?
3.c: 2017 WAO Pkt Carson et al Q18

3.q: A 2023 reinterpretation of this album features the tracks "Raven Flies Low" and "Mor Ning Prayers", and features artists such as Benji B and Nubya Garcia. Radiohead lead singer Thom ("tom")Yorke cited this album as the initial inspiration for their album OK Computer. The only track not to feature the bandleader on this album is named after, and heavily features, the guitarist (*) John McLaughlin. Bennie Maupin plays bass clarinet on the 27 minute title track of this album and one titled for the bandleader who "Runs the Voodoo Down". Wayne Shorter wrote this album's song "Sanctuary". This album was the second by its bandleader to feature Chick Corea and Joe Zawinul, the latter of whom wrote the opening track Pharaoh's Dance. For 10 points, name this 1970 jazz fusion album by Miles Davis.
3.r: Bitches Brew [anti-prompt on London Brew by asking “what earlier album did this pay tribute to?”]

3.q: An artist who gained fame in this city in the 1980s once almost crashed a plane because he convinced himself that he was Casper the Friendly Ghost. That subject of a Jeff Feuerzeig documentary entitled The Devil and [his name] made a mural in this city replicating an album cover of his featuring a frog with long eyes and the words, "Hi, How Are You?" This city was the longtime home of the schizophrenic singer-songwriter behind the song "True Love Will Find You in the End," (*) Daniel Johnston. It also produced a band who wrote a song that opens, "Remember the weight of the world, it's a sound that we used to buy on cassette and 45." Another song by that band from this city states, "Life can be so fair, let it go on and on." "I Summon You" and "You Got Yr. Cherry Bomb," are songs by a Britt Daniel-fronted band from this city called Spoon. For 10 points, name this city that hosts a film, media, and music festival called South by Southwest and is home to the University of Texas.

A drumming style from this country uses three drums called harps, including the thunder drum and repeater. The first Black-owned recording studio in this country, Studio One, was founded by producer Coxsone Dodd. The chorus of a song partly titled for this country begins with the lines "But I'm sad to say I'm on my way / Won't be back for many a day." This country's "rocksteady" music gave rise to the "dancehall" genre of the 1970s. Rap evolved from a 1950s musical style from this country in which a (*) deejay talks over a beat, called "toasting." A song from this country's "mento" genre that includes the refrain "Daylight come and me wan' go home" was recorded by an American singer whose family was from here, Harry Belafonte. For 10 points, name this country where reggae was popularized by Bob Marley.
3.c: 2025 IQBT Undergraduate Championship Pkt 06 - Prelims 6 Q5

3.q: In a song whose title ends with this word, the melody of the A section begins with syncopated eighth-notes E-flat, D, C repeated for several bars; that work was composed by Euday Bowman. Wilbur Sweatman composed a song whose title contains this word after the words "Down Home." The Mills Brothers' first single was a cover of a song whose title ends with this word. Another composition with this word in its title is named for the (*) "snake" figure played by King Oliver and Louis Armstrong. This is the last word in the title of a standard whose lyrics repeat the phrase "Hold that tiger" several times. For 10 points, name this word that appears in the titles of many Scott Joplin compositions.

This artist developed the dissonant "Willisau chord" during his performance at the 2000 Willisau Jazz Festival. This artist was the subject of an experimental five-part exhibition at the Whitney titled Open Plan, where he performed alongside dancer Min Tanaka and drummer Tony Oxley. In Ken Burns: Jazz, Branford Marsalis referred to this musician's philosophy as "total self-indulgent bullshit." This author of the essay "Sound Structure of Subculture Becoming Major Breath/Naked Fire Gesture" included his song "Rick Kick Shaw" and a cover of Thelonious Monk's "Bemsha Swing" on his 1956 album (*) Jazz Advance. This artist dedicated his live album For Olim to his longtime collaborator Jimmy Lyons. "Enter Evening" and "Steps" are by, for 10 points, which free jazz pianist who recorded the album Unit Structures?

Charles Lloyd plays the melody of "Matchmaker" on a flute on the final track of an album led by this musician, presenting jazz reworkings of songs from Fiddler on the Roof. The composer of the musical Hair, Galt MacDermot, won his first Grammy Award for the title track of an album by this musician, titled African Waltz. This man was the musician added to the Miles Davis Quintet to make it a sextet on the album Milestones. A live recording this musician made in 1959 at The Jazz Workshop, titled for his quintet "in San Francisco," was a watershed moment in the popularization of (*) "soul jazz." That style is also found on a song that Joe Zawinul wrote for him, titled "Mercy, Mercy, Mercy," which he recorded with his younger brother, a cornetist and trumpeter named Nat. For 10 points, name this hard bop-era saxophonist nicknamed "Cannonball."

It's not Wayne Shorter, but one of this artist's albums is bookended by covers of Baden Powell's "Samba em Preludio" and Milton Nascimento's "Ponta de Areia." Leo Genovese played piano on three of this artist's albums. This artist included a cover of Michael Jackson's song "I Can't Help It" on a 2012 album. Algebra Blessett and Lionel Loueke are featured on a song by this artist whose lyrics state "Hold your head as high as you can / High enough to see who you are, little man." Each of the tracks of this artist's most recent album, (*) 12 Little Spells, corresponds to a part of the body. The tracks "Judas" and "Earth to Heaven" are included on a 2016 album by this artist, Emily's D+Evolution. The album Radio Music Society is by, For 10 points, what former child prodigy and Grammy-winning bassist?

This noun appears in the title of an album whose penultimate track's instrumentation includes tabla, soprano saxophone, and mandocello ("man-doh-CHELL-oh"). This noun partly titles a film in which the Nicholas Brothers perform "Jumpin' Jive," accompanied by Cab Calloway & His Orchestra. Lena Horne sings the title Harold Arlen song in that film, which is partly named for this noun, and which, along with Cabin in the Sky, was one of the first two mainstream movie musicals to have an (*) all-Black cast. This noun appears in the title of an album that closes with the track "Havona" and opens with the track "Birdland." That album is by a band with this first title word, which was co-founded by Wayne Shorter. For 10 points, a jazz fusion band co-founded by Joe Zawinul ("ZOV-in-ul") is named for what kind of "report"?

A song by this composer uses the words "down deep in my heart" on the five-note melody: short F, then triplet 'F, D-sharp, E' then long G; and ends by saying "the music is sweet, the words are true." The initial A section of a song by this composer opens by moving from F minor 7 to B-flat minor 7 to E-flat dominant 7 to A-flat major 7, and the A2 section repeats those chords transposed down a fourth. Otto Harbach wrote the lines "they asked me how I knew my true love was true" to open a song by this composer originally written for the musical Roberta; that song became a huge hit for The Platters and was called "Smoke Gets In Your Eyes." This composer's musical Very Warm for May includes the song (*) "All the Things You Are." Paul Robeson famously sang a song by this composer performed alongside a chorus of dock workers. For 10 points, name this composer who wrote the song "Ol' Man River" for the musical Show Boat.

This musician and a keyboardist wrote the music for the Steppenwolf productions of the Lyle Kessler play Orphans. This musician collaborated with his brother Mike, a flugelhornist, on the album Secret Story. This musician, the only person to win Grammys in 10 different categories, composed much of his music alongside keyboardist Lyle Mays. The first recording of Steve Reich's Electric Counterpoint was performed by this musician. The first recording of bassist Jaco ("JAH-co") Pastorious was a collaborative album with this musician, who later worked with Pastorious on his debut album (*) Bright Size Life. This musician's unique instruments include the Pickasso, a custom-made instrument with 42 strings. For 10 points, name this jazz fusion musician, known for using the 12-string guitar on recordings like signature song "Last Train Home" with his namesake "Group."
3.c: 2022 Chicago Open Pkt 02 Fine + Cummings + Friedman Q2

3.q: A musician who played this instrument recorded "In the Kitchen" with Eddie "Lockjaw" Davis and was known as the "Queen of" this instrument. A musician who plays this instrument named Pat Bianchi played in a trio with guitarist Pat Martino. This is the main instrument played by the musicians Joey DeFrancesco and his father "Papa" John. The usage of this instrument in a jazz trio was pioneered by a musician who formed his own trio with Chris Columbus and Bill Jennings named Wild Bill Davis. The Stanley Turrentine tune "Minor Chant" appears on an album by a bandleader who played this instrument titled Back to the (*) Chicken Shack. The centrality of this instrument was one of the defining characteristics separating soul jazz from its origins in hard bop. Jimmy Smith played this instrument, as did a musician who led the group who released the song "Green Onions." For 10 points, Laurens Hammond designed a popular electric version of what keyboard instrument?
3.r: jazz organ [or electric organ; accept Hammond organ; prompt on Hammond before mention; prompt on keyboards before mention; reject “pipe organ” or “reed organ” or “electric piano”]
3.c: 2022 Chicago Open Pkt 03 Nguyen + Marvin + Lifshitz Q17

3.q: Note: answering with either the bandleader or band is acceptable. This band repurposed the Beatles song "Lucy In The Sky With Diamonds" into the track "Reflections of Lucy," which appears on their self-titled album. It's not the Dave Matthews Band, but this band's album Left of Cool was the first to feature saxophonist Jeff Coffin. This band included the tracks "The Yee-Haw Factor" and "Sex in a Pan" on a 1993 album with a palindromic title. Howard Levy plays double ocarina on this band's song "Hole in the Wall." A member of this band known for wearing a pirate hat on stage plays the SynthAxe (*) Drumitar. That musician, who goes by the nickname "Future Man," is brothers with this band's bassist, Victor Wooten. This band released the albums UFO Tofu and Flight of the Cosmic Hippo. For 10 points, name this progressive jazz group led by a banjoist.

In 1963, John Coltrane and this musician recorded a track he composed whose original D minor version's bridge repeats a D-flat major 1-6-2-5 chord progression, and whose melody opens like Gershwin's "Someone to Watch Over Me" with a rising 6-note F major pentatonic pickup and long high G. Lorenzo Tio's "Mexican Blues" inspired a standard he wrote with Barney Bigard that swapped the trombone and clarinet's registers to create a "mike-tone." Early in his career, his band's signature song was "East St. Louis Toodle-Oo," an example of his (*) "jungle music." His career was revived after he had Paul Gonsalves play a 27-bar saxophone solo during a performance of "Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue" at the 1956 Newport Jazz Festival. He composed the standards "In a Sentimental Mood" and "Mood Indigo." For 10 points, name this jazz pianist who often performed Billy Strayhorn's "Take the 'A' Train."

The original version of a song whose title begins with this word was performed by a seven-piece ensemble, in which a muted trumpet and a high muted trombone double the melody. The B-side of another song whose title ends with this word is a version of Vincent Youmans' "I Want to Be Happy." The album Masterpieces by Ellington opens with a 15-minute version of a song whose title begins with this word. In the key of A-flat major, a song whose title begins with this word opens with the melody "C, (*) B-natural, C, C." "Tar Paper Stomp" by Wingy Manone formed the basis for a 1939 single whose title ends with this word. A song whose title begins with this word has a melody that was borrowed from Lorenzo Tio, and was first recorded by Duke Ellington in 1930. In the title of a jazz standard, for 10 points, what word precedes "Indigo"?

The song "Soldier" by Ruslan Sirota opens a Grammy-winning album titled for a bassist with this first name who was a founding member of Chick Corea's Return to Forever. Bob Graettinger's avant-garde pieces fill the album City of Glass by a pianist with this first name whose orchestra won Grammys for Adventures in Jazz and a jazz rendition of West Side Story. With Charlie Byrd, a saxophonist with this first name created a version of "Desafinado" on the album Jazz Samba. Namesake band (*) clinics were launched by a pianist with this first name and surname Kenton. Astrud Gilberto ("ZHEEL-behr-too") sang on a recording of a song by a musician with this first name on an album named for him and Joao Gilberto. Songs including "Corcovado" and "The Girl From Ipanema" were performed by a saxophonist with, for 10 points, what first name and surname Getz?
3.r: Stan [or Stanley; or Stan Getz; or Stan Kenton; or Stanley Clarke]

3.q: He's not Thad Jones or PDQ Bach, but this musician followed up an eccentric solo by Dannie Richmond with a solo in which he quoted "Pop Goes the Weasel." That solo was played on the tune "So Long Eric," during a concert performance with the Charles Mingus Sextet. This musician released the album Caribe with the Latin Jazz Quintet, and played a non-standard jazz instrument on the Ornette Coleman album Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation.
